title: Failure of time constructibility
statement: Define $T(n)=n+1$ if the halting predicate for the fixed time-hierarchy code accepts the binary string associated to $n$, and define $T(n)=n$ otherwise. Then $T$ is not time-constructible: it is false that both $n\le T(n)$ for every natural number $n$ and that there exist a positive natural number $c$ and a finite-state Turing machine $M$ over the binary alphabet such that, for every finite binary input $x$, $M$ halts with output the binary expansion of $T(|x|)$ within $c(T(|x|)+1)$ steps.
hypotheses_covered: $T$ is the specified function defined using the fixed time-hierarchy code and its halting predicate
replaced:
Fix an effective coding of binary Turing machines, with a decoder that assigns a machine
to every binary string, and let $H(s)$ be true exactly when $s$ encodes a machine
description followed by an input on which the decoded machine halts. For each
$n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $w_n$ be the binary bit list of $n+1$ with its last bit removed,
and define $T(n)=n+1$ if $H(w_n)$ is true and $T(n)=n$ otherwise. There is no positive
integer $c$ and no finite-state Turing machine over the binary alphabet that, on every
binary input $x$, halts with output the binary expansion of $T(|x|)$ within
$c(T(|x|)+1)$ steps while $n\leq T(n)$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
